about: Close ingredient swaps for the recipe book: how much of one replaces the other, how alike they are, and what changes. A side with a unit ("clove", "tsp") is for swaps that change unit.

b.name: chickpea
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred chickpeas, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: butter bean
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred butter beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are creamier and often salted.

b.name: cannellini bean
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred cannellini beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: haricot bean
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred haricot beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: white beans
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred white beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: black beans
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred black beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: borlotti bean
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned or jarred borlotti beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained, roughly one 400g tin. Jarred are softer and often salted, so season at the end.

b.name: red kidney beans
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
b.label: tinned red kidney beans, drained

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives about 240g drained. Dried must be soaked, then boiled hard for 10 minutes before simmering.

b.name: puy lentil
b.form: tin or tinned or pouch or cooked or ready-cooked or jar
b.label: ready-cooked puy lentils

swaps.note: Weight only. 100g dried gives roughly 250g cooked. Ready-cooked are softer; add them near the end just to heat through.
Use the same form, dried or tinned. Butter beans are bigger and creamier.
Use the same form. Haricot are smaller; both are mild white beans.
Use the same form. Borlotti are creamier and nuttier; cannellini are milder.
Use the same form. Kidney beans are firmer with thicker skins. Dried kidney beans need a 10-minute hard boil.

a.name: chickpea
a.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked or pouch
a.label: tinned chickpeas

b.name: cannellini bean
b.form: tin or tinned or jar or jarred or can or canned or cooked
b.label: tinned cannellini beans

swaps.note: Drained weight for drained weight. Cannellini are softer and creamier, so they won't roast crisp. Fine in stews and dips.
Use the same form. Green lentils turn soft and lose their shape sooner, so cook them a little less.
Use the same form. Both hold their shape and taste earthy.
Both are ground chickpeas. Gram flour is made from split brown chickpeas and is often finer; they behave the same.

a.name: parsley
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh parsley

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried tastes of little; add it while cooking, never as a garnish.

a.name: basil
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh basil

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried is flat and minty; add it early in sauces, never raw.

a.name: dill
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh dill

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried works in dressings left to stand; weak scattered on at the end.

a.name: mint
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh mint

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried suits yoghurt sauces and cooked dishes, not salads.

a.name: thyme
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh thyme

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried thyme keeps its flavour well; add it early so it softens.

a.name: oregano
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh oregano

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried oregano is often preferred in cooked tomato sauces.

a.name: rosemary
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh rosemary

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Crumble dried needles finely and add them early so they soften.

a.name: sage
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh sage

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried is mustier; fine in stuffings and stews, not for frying whole leaves.

a.name: tarragon
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh tarragon

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried loses much of the aniseed; best in sauces.

a.name: mixed herbs
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh mixed herbs

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp chopped fresh ≈ 1 tsp dried. Dried suit long cooking, not finishing a dish.
Count for count, fresh leaves are stronger: 1 fresh does the work of 2 dried.
Dried leaves lose much of their aroma, so use about twice as many. Frozen fresh leaves keep far better.
Spoon for spoon, finely sliced, not count for count. Spring onion tops are a little stronger and crunchier.

a.name: coriander
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh coriander

swaps.note: Gives the green colour and freshness, not the citrus taste. Useful for anyone who dislikes coriander.
Curly parsley is a little more bitter and chewier; chop it finely.

b.name: basil
b.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
b.label: Italian basil

swaps.note: Thai basil tastes of aniseed and stands up to heat. Italian basil is sweeter; add it at the very end.

a.name: dill
a.form: fresh or sprig or sprigs or bunch or handful or leaves or chopped or picked
a.label: fresh dill

swaps.note: Same amount, chopped. Fennel fronds are milder with more aniseed.
Use the same form, fresh or dried. Marjoram is milder and sweeter than oregano.
By weight or spoon for spoon. Toasted seeds give pops of flavour; ground blends in but burns fast, so add it later.
By weight; spoon for spoon is close enough. Freshly ground toasted seeds taste brighter than shop-bought ground.
By weight or spoon for spoon. Whole seeds give bursts of aniseed; ground spreads evenly through the dish.
By weight. Whole peppercorns suit stocks and brines; ground pepper clouds a stock and tastes stronger there.
Spoon for spoon. Freshly grated is brighter; ready-ground fades with age.
Spoon for spoon. Brown seeds are very slightly milder; both pop in hot oil.
Spoon for spoon. Yellow seeds are noticeably milder and don't pop as much.
Spoon for spoon. You lose the smoky flavour, which often defines the dish.
Spoon for spoon. Curry powder has turmeric, chilli and fenugreek; garam masala is warmer and sweeter.
Same amount. White pepper is earthier and sharper, and doesn't speckle pale sauces.

a.name: ginger
a.form: fresh or grated or piece or thumb or cm or root or knob or peeled
a.label: fresh ginger, grated

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp grated fresh ≈ ¼ tsp ground. A thumb-sized piece gives about 1 tbsp. Ground is warmer, less zingy.

a.name: ginger
a.form: fresh or grated or piece or thumb or cm or root or knob or peeled
a.label: fresh ginger, grated

b.name: ginger
b.form: paste or jar or jarred or puree or purée
b.label: ginger paste

swaps.note: Spoon for spoon, grated fresh to paste. Jarred paste often contains salt and acid, so it tastes flatter.

a.name: turmeric
a.form: fresh or grated or piece or thumb or cm or root or knob or peeled
a.label: fresh turmeric, grated

swaps.note: Spoon only: 1 tbsp grated fresh ≈ 1 tsp ground. Fresh is brighter and more peppery. Both stain.
Changes unit: per clove, use about ¼ tsp granules. Add with liquid so they don't burn. Flatter, sweeter taste.
Changes unit: per clove, use about ⅛ tsp powder. Add with liquid so it doesn't burn or clump.
Changes unit: per chilli, about ½ tsp flakes. Chillies vary a lot in heat, so add half, taste, then the rest.
Spoon only: cayenne is fine and packs densely, so use about half. It blends in with no flecks.
Spoon for spoon with hot chilli powder. Some blends contain cumin or garlic; mild ones need more.
Count for count. Green chillies taste grassier, red fruitier; heat depends on the variety, so taste.
Count for count. Jalapeños are fatter and usually milder than thin green chillies; taste and adjust.
Count for count. Similar fierce heat and fruity flavour. Wear gloves.

b.name: chilli flakes
b.label: chilli flakes, plus a pinch of smoked paprika

swaps.note: Plain flakes are usually hotter and lack smoke, so use half as much and add a pinch of smoked paprika.
Spoon for spoon. Rose harissa has a floral note. Jars vary a lot in heat, so taste first.
Spoon for spoon. Sriracha is thicker, sweeter and garlicky; vinegar-based hot sauces are thinner and sharper.
Weight only, cooked dishes only: a 400g tin for about 400g ripe tomatoes. Fresh need longer cooking down.
Tin for tin. Crush whole plum tomatoes by hand; they're often sweeter and less watery.
Tin for tin. Tinned cherry tomatoes are sweeter and hold their shape.
Weight or volume. Passata is smooth and sieved, so the sauce has no chunks.
1 part purée plus 3 parts water ≈ 4 parts passata. Purée tastes more cooked; reduce passata down to replace purée.
The same product: UK tomato purée is what other countries call tomato paste.
Spoon for spoon. Sun-dried paste is sweeter, oilier and more intense.
Weight for weight. Cherry tomatoes are sweeter and juicier; halve them rather than chop.
Full-fat crème fraîche can boil without splitting and adds tang. It won't whip stiff like double cream.
Single cream is thinner, splits if boiled and won't whip. Fine stirred into sauces off the heat.
Whipping cream is lighter. It whips well but makes thinner, less rich sauces.
Soured cream is tangier and thinner, and splits if boiled. Stir it in off the heat.
Yoghurt is tangier and splits if boiled. Stir it in off the heat, or mix in a little cornflour first.
Greek yoghurt is thicker and slightly sharper. Both split if boiled.
Natural yoghurt is thinner and sharper. Strain it in a sieve lined with kitchen paper to thicken.
Labneh is thicker and saltier. Loosen it with a little water or milk if needed.
Coconut yoghurt is dairy-free, sweeter, tastes of coconut and is often thinner.
Coconut cream is dairy-free but tastes of coconut, so it suits curries and soups more than delicate sauces.
Coconut cream is richer and thicker. Thin it with a splash of water for a lighter sauce.
Light coconut milk is thinner and less rich. Simmer a little longer to thicken.
Drain cottage cheese, then blitz or sieve it smooth. It's saltier and wetter.
Cream cheese is tangier and less rich. Fine in icings and baked dishes.
Pecorino is saltier and sharper, so season less. Grate it finely.
Grana padano is milder and slightly softer. Use the same weight.
Parmesan is made with animal rennet, so isn't vegetarian. The Italian-style hard cheese is slightly milder.
Manchego is milder and less salty. Grate finely and add a pinch of salt if needed.
Crumbly goat's cheese is closest. Soft goat's cheese is creamier and less salty.
Both fry without melting. Paneer is milder and unsalted, so season it well.
Tofu is dairy-free. Press it first. It's softer and blander, so season or marinate it well.
Burrata is creamier and wetter. Tear it over at the end; don't bake it.
Both melt well. Gruyère is nuttier and sweeter; cheddar is sharper.
Very similar Alpine cheeses. Use the same weight.
Emmental is milder and melts more stringily.
Same amount. Fine in sauces and baking; slightly sweet and thinner.
Same amount. Holds up well in sauces; can curdle in very acidic dishes.
For frying and curries. Ghee has no water or milk solids, so it gets hotter without burning.
For frying, roasting and mash, not pastry or creaming. Butter is about 80% fat, so use four-fifths as much oil.
Use a block, not a spread, for baking. Choose unsalted if you can.
Coconut oil is dairy-free. Butter is about 80% fat, so use four-fifths as much coconut oil. Use it solid for pastry and crumble.
Same amount. Cold-pressed rapeseed is buttery and nutty; olive oil is fruitier.
Plain olive oil is milder. Fine for cooking; extra virgin is better for dressings and drizzling.
Same amount. Sunflower is neutral; cold-pressed rapeseed tastes nutty.
Both neutral. Same amount for frying, roasting and baking.
UK vegetable oil is usually rapeseed oil. Same amount.
Both neutral and good for high heat. Same amount for stir-frying.
Sunflower oil is a neutral oil. Same amount.
Same amount. Coconut oil is solid when cool and may taste of coconut unless refined.
Spoon for spoon. Lime is more fragrant and slightly more bitter; lemon is rounder.
Count: a lemon gives about 3 tbsp juice, a lime about 2. Lime zest is more fragrant.
Spoon for spoon in dressings and marinades. Vinegar has no fruitiness; add a pinch of sugar if harsh.
Same amount. White is a little lighter and won't colour the dish.
Same amount. Cider vinegar is fruitier and slightly milder.
Same amount. Sherry vinegar is rounder and nuttier.
The same thing under two names.

b.name: white wine vinegar
b.label: white wine vinegar, plus a pinch of sugar

swaps.note: Wine vinegar is sharper: three parts replace four of rice vinegar. Add a pinch of sugar.

b.name: red wine vinegar
b.label: red wine vinegar, plus a pinch of sugar

swaps.note: Balsamic is sweet and syrupy; red wine vinegar is sharp. Sweeten it with a pinch of sugar.
Same amount. Vermouth is more herbal and keeps for months once opened.
Spoon for spoon. Maple is thinner and less sweet, with a caramel taste, and vegan.
Spoon for spoon. Agave is thinner, neutral-tasting and vegan.
Spoon for spoon. Golden syrup tastes of caramel rather than flowers.
Spoon for spoon. Agave is a little sweeter, with no caramel taste.
Spoon for spoon in dressings and sauces. Not for baking, where the extra liquid changes the result.
Same weight. Granulated is coarser; for meringues and sponges, blitz it fine first.
Same weight. Golden caster has a faint caramel note and slightly darker colour.
Same weight. Muscovado is moister with a deeper toffee taste.
Spoon for spoon. Paste adds the black specks; extract is thinner.
Add 1 level tsp baking powder per 100g plain flour. Use self-raising for plain only in bakes with baking powder, leaving that out.
Thickening only: plain flour has half the thickening power, so use twice as much and simmer a few minutes longer.
Same weight. Spelt dough is more fragile, so knead it less. Wholemeal spelt needs a little more liquid.
Same weight. Fine for sauces and batters; bakes may be crumblier.
For crisp coatings and batters, same weight. Rice flour gives a lighter, crunchier crust.
Bicarb is about four times stronger and needs an acid such as yoghurt or lemon juice. Too much tastes soapy.
Spoon for spoon, not by weight: panko is airier. It gives a lighter, crunchier crust.
Any good crusty loaf works. Sourdough is chewier and tangier.
Pitta is thicker and has a pocket. Warm it before serving.
Naan is softer and richer. Warm either through before serving.
Flour tortillas are softer and bigger; corn ones are more fragile and taste of maize.
Changes unit: per cube, about 2 tsp powder. Most cubes and 2 tsp powder each make 500ml, but brands vary; check the pack.
Same form and amount. Vegetable stock is lighter and keeps the dish vegetarian.
Weight only. A medium onion is about 150g, a banana shallot about 50g. Shallots are milder and sweeter.
Count for count. Red onions are milder and sweeter raw; cooked, they're close but tint the dish.
Count for count. White onions are a little sharper raw; cooked, much the same.
Weight only, trimmed: use the white and pale green. Leeks are milder and sweeter; wash out any grit.
Weight only. Good raw or pickled; shallots are milder and finer. A red onion is about 150g, a banana shallot 50g.
Same amount as a topping. Shop-bought crispy onions are sweeter and saltier.

a.name: spinach
a.form: fresh or bag or leaves or baby
a.label: fresh spinach

swaps.note: Weight only: about 300g frozen for 500g fresh. Thaw and squeeze out the water. For cooking, not salads.
Weight for weight. Chop and cook chard stalks a few minutes first; the leaves wilt like spinach.
Weight for weight, for cooking. Strip the tough stems; kale needs several minutes longer and stays chewy.
Weight for weight. Strip kale stems and cook it a few minutes longer; chard is softer.
Weight for weight. Cavolo nero is darker, sweeter and more tender. Strip the stems of both.
Weight for weight. Strip the cavolo nero stems and cook it a little longer than chard leaves.
Weight for weight, shredded. Spring greens are more tender, so cook them a little less.
Weight for weight, shredded. Savoy is crinklier and slightly sweeter.
Same weight. Savoy is more tender and cooks faster.
Same weight. White is milder and won't colour the dish; red needs a little acid to stay purple.
Same amount. Both peppery; watercress is softer and wilts faster, so dress it just before serving.
Same weight. Trim woody ends; cook both briefly. Purple sprouting has a deeper flavour.
Same weight. Cut a head into long florets and slice the stalk so they cook in a similar time.
Same weight. String runners and slice them thinly on the diagonal. They're coarser and take a little longer.
Weight for weight, peeled. Dense pumpkins like crown prince are closest; watery carving pumpkins are poor.
Weight for weight, peeled. Sweet potato is sweeter and softer, and cooks a little faster.

b.name: fennel
b.form: bulb or fresh or sliced or chopped
b.label: fennel bulb

swaps.note: Same weight, raw or cooked. Fennel adds an aniseed flavour.
Same weight and cooking. Romanesco is firmer and nuttier.
Same podded weight. Frozen peas are often sweeter than shop-bought fresh ones.
Same weight, drained or thawed. Frozen is slightly firmer.
The same lettuce under two names.
Both bitter. Chicory is milder and crunchier.
Count for count. Yellow and orange are as sweet as red; only the colour changes.
Count for count. Green peppers are unripe, so more bitter and less sweet.
Same weight. Both hold their shape when boiled; new potatoes are smaller with thinner skins.
Same weight. Baking potatoes are floury varieties, good for mash and roasties.
Weight only: 10g dried for about 80g fresh. Dried porcini are far more intense; keep their soaking liquid.
Same dried weight, soaked. Shiitake are smokier and less earthy. Keep the soaking liquid.
Same weight. Button mushrooms are milder and wetter; fry them hard to drive off the water.
Same weight. Portobellos are grown-up chestnut mushrooms; cut them to the same size.
Same weight. Oyster mushrooms are softer and cook faster; tear rather than slice.
Same weight. Shiitake are meatier and stronger; remove the tough stalks.
Same count or weight. Both are large flat mushrooms for grilling or stuffing.
Same weight, toasted. Cashews are creamier and sweeter; good in pesto.
Same weight, toasted. Walnuts are more bitter; good in pesto.
Sunflower seeds are nut-free. Same weight, toasted. They taste slightly earthier.
Same weight. Pecans are sweeter and less bitter.
Same weight and form, toasted. Almonds are milder.
Same weight. Almonds are milder and you lose the green colour.
Same weight, toasted. Sunflower seeds are smaller and milder.
Same amount. Black sesame are earthier and slightly bitter; mostly for looks.
Same weight. Cashews are sweeter and softer.
Same amount. Almond butter is milder and often runnier.
Same amount. Milder and sweeter than tahini; add a little extra lemon. Works in dressings and hummus.

a.name: basmati rice
a.form: uncooked or raw or dry or dried
a.label: uncooked basmati rice

swaps.note: Weight only: rice weighs roughly 2½ times as much once cooked. Leftover cooked rice is best for fried rice.

a.name: jasmine rice
a.form: uncooked or raw or dry or dried
a.label: uncooked jasmine rice

swaps.note: Weight only: rice weighs roughly 2½ times as much once cooked. Chill leftovers quickly.
Same weight. Jasmine is softer and slightly sticky with a floral smell; basmati grains stay separate.
Same weight. Long-grain rice is less fragrant; cook it the same way.
Same weight. Brown rice takes about twice as long and needs more water. It's nuttier and chewier.
Same weight. Check the packet for cooking time.
Same weight. Tagliatelle is narrower; check the packet for cooking time.
Same weight. Small shells catch the sauce in the same way; check the cooking time.
Same weight. Check the packet for cooking time.
Same weight. Both are small pasta; giant couscous is rounder and chewier.
Same weight. Spelt is nuttier and cooks a little faster.
Same weight. Couscous only needs soaking in boiling water and is softer; bulgur needs longer.
Same weight. Extra-firm needs little or no pressing.
Same weight. Smoked tofu is firmer and already flavoured, so season the dish less.
Same weight. Tempeh is denser and nuttier. Steam it for 10 minutes first to soften any bitterness.
Same weight. Soft tofu is slightly firmer; both blend into sauces and desserts.
Red miso is saltier and stronger, so use about half as much as white. White is sweeter.
Same amount. Tamari is usually gluten-free (check the label) and a little richer.
Dark soy is thicker, sweeter and less salty, mainly for colour; light soy is saltier. Season to taste.
Same amount. Coconut aminos is sweeter and much less salty; add a pinch of salt.
Same amount. Soy sauce is less funky and slightly sweeter; add a squeeze of lime.
Spoon only: flakes are lighter, so 2 spoons of flakes match 1 of fine. By weight they're equally salty.
Same amount. Wholegrain is milder and seedy; Dijon is smoother and sharper.
English mustard is much hotter, so use about half as much.
Same amount, chopped. Olives give a similar briny, salty hit.
Same amount. Black olives are milder and softer.
Same amount. Kalamatas are fruitier and more winey; plain pitted black olives are milder.
Same amount. Kimchi is spicy and garlicky; sauerkraut is plainly sour.
Same weight. Trout is milder and thinner, so it cooks faster.
Same weight; flake it the same way. Trout is slightly milder.
